questions.question: What are semantic HTML5 elements? List the main ones and their purposes.
questions.title: HTML5 Semantic Elements — header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer
questions.direct_answer:
What are semantic HTML5 elements? List the main ones and their purposes.

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser pipeline, framework hooks, and user-visible outcomes), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Main semantic elements (header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer, figure, figcaption, time, mark) and their purposes.

**Classic weak answer:** Using <section> as a generic container — it must have a heading; prefer <div> when no section label is meaningful.

**Senior finish:** Contrast semantic vs generic (div/span); note that semantics help SEO and assistive tech without extra ARIA.

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **HTML5 Semantic Elements — header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** What are semantic HTML5 elements? List the main ones and their purposes.

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Main semantic elements (header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer, figure, figcaption, time, mark) and their purposes**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Using <section> as a generic container — it must have a heading; prefer <div> when no section label is meaningful**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Contrast semantic vs generic (div/span); note that semantics help SEO and assistive tech without extra ARIA**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Main semantic elements (header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer, figure, figcaption, time, mark) and their purposes
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).


sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **using <section> as a generic container — it must have a heading; prefer <div> when no section label is meaningful** and what you do instead.

sections.content:

**Body (45–60 seconds):** Walk through **Main semantic elements (header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer, figure, figcaption, time, mark) and their purposes** as a story: what runs, what breaks, what you log/measure.

**Pitfall (15 seconds):** Call out **Using <section> as a generic container — it must have a heading; prefer <div> when no section label is meaningful** — interviewers reward honesty about real bugs.

**Finish (15–20 seconds):** Add **Contrast semantic vs generic (div/span); note that semantics help SEO and assistive tech without extra ARIA**, then offer a trade-off question back (“do you optimize for TTFB or TTI here?”).

questions.question: What is semantic HTML and why should you use it instead of div-heavy markup?
questions.title: Semantic HTML vs div-Only Markup — Why Semantics Matter
questions.direct_answer:
What is semantic HTML and why should you use it instead of div-heavy markup?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser pipeline, framework hooks, and user-visible outcomes), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Accessibility (screen-reader landmarks), SEO (better crawling), maintainability (self-documenting), and CSS-less styling hints.

**Classic weak answer:** Wrapping every piece of content in nested divs — it loses default semantics and forces ARIA to recreate what HTML already provides.

**Senior finish:** Mention WCAG landmarks, tabindex on non-interactive divs (wrong), and the 'first rule of ARIA' (don't use ARIA if a native element exists).
